rootMfaActive.^description: Root user can perform sensitive operations in your account, adding an additional layer of authentication helps you to better secure your account. You have NOT enabled Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on your root user. AWS MFA is a simple best practice that adds an extra layer of protection on top of your user name and password. With MFA enabled, when a user signs in to an AWS Management Console, they will be prompted for their user name and password (the first factor—what they know), as well as for an authentication code from their AWS MFA device (the second factor—what they have). Taken together, these multiple factors provide increased security for your AWS account settings and resources.

mfaActive.^description: You have not enabled Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on {$COUNT} IAM users. AWS MFA is a simple best practice that adds an extra layer of protection on top of your user name and password. With MFA enabled, when a user signs in to an AWS Management Console, they will be prompted for their user name and password (the first factor—what they know), as well as for an authentication code from their AWS MFA device (the second factor—what they have). Taken together, these multiple factors provide increased security for your AWS account settings and resources.

passwordLastChange365.^description: {$COUNT} IAM user passwords have not been changed in more than 365 days. Please rotate the passwords. Alternatively, you can set an expiration period in the password policy.

passwordLastChange90.^description: {$COUNT} IAM user passwords have not been changed in more than 90 days. Please rotate the passwords. Alternatively, you can set an expiration period in the password policy.

consoleLastAccess365.^description: {$COUNT} IAM users have not accessed the AWS console in more than 365 days. Please identify the need for these IAM users to access the console and delete them if not needed.

consoleLastAccess90.^description: {$COUNT} IAM users have not accessed the AWS console in more than 90 days. Please identify the need for these IAM users to access the console and delete them if not needed.

consoleLastAccess45.^description: {$COUNT} IAM users have not accessed the AWS console in more than 45 days. Please identify the need for these IAM users to access the console and delete them if not needed.

passwordPolicy.^description: You have not set a custom password policy. Setting a custom password policy will allow you to have the ability to require strong password practices, such as complexity level, avoiding re-use, and enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA). If you don't set a custom password policy, IAM user passwords must meet the default AWS password policy.

passwordPolicyWeak.^description: Your current password policy is not strong. Improving the strength of your password policy would improve the security of your account. Consider implementing best practices when setting the password policy. If you already configure as per your organization

passwordPolicyReuse.^description: Your current password policy is not strong. Improving the strength of your password policy would improve the security of your account. Consider implementing best practices when setting the password policy. If you already configure as per your organization

passwordPolicyLength.^description: Your current password policy is not strong. Improving the strength of your password policy would improve the security of your account. Consider implementing best practices when setting the password policy. If you already configure as per your organization

InlinePolicy.^description: You have set an inline policy for {$COUNT} IAM users, groups or roles. An inline policy is a policy that's embedded in an IAM identity (a user, group, or role). In most cases, we recommend that you use managed policies instead of inline policies. This is because managed policies have several additional features such as reusability, central change management, versioning and rolling back, delegating permissions management and automatic updates. Inline policies are useful if you want to maintain a strict one-to-one relationship between a policy and the identity that it's applied to. For example, you want to be sure that the permissions in a policy are not inadvertently assigned to an identity other than the one they're intended for.

InlinePolicyFullAccessOneServ.^description: You have set an inline policy giving {$COUNT} users, groups and/or roles full access to one service. Consider switching to managed policies instead. It is also considered best practice to limit access by following the standard security advice of granting least privilege, or granting only the permissions required to perform a task. Determine what users and roles need to do and then craft policies that allow them to perform only those tasks.

InlinePolicyFullAdminAccess.^description: You have set an inline policy providing full Administrator access to {$COUNT} users, groups or roles. It is considered best practice to limit access by following the standard security advice of granting least privilege, or granting only the permissions required to perform a task. Determine what users and roles need to do and then craft policies that allow them to perform only those tasks.

ManagedPolicyFullAccessOneServ.^description: You have set a managed policy giving {$COUNT} users, groups and/or roles full access to one service. It is considered best practice to limit access by following the standard security advice of granting least privilege, or granting only the permissions required to perform a task. Determine what users and roles need to do and then craft policies that allow them to perform only those tasks.

FullAdminAccess.^description: You have provided full Administrator access to {$COUNT} users, groups or roles. It is considered best practice to limit access by following the standard security advice of granting least privilege, or granting only the permissions required to perform a task. Determine what users and roles need to do and then craft policies that allow them to perform only those tasks.

userNotUsingGroup.^description: {$COUNT} users are not within user groups. An IAM user group is a collection of IAM users. User groups let you specify permissions for multiple users, which can make it easier to manage the permissions for those users.
userNotUsingGroup.shortDesc: Place IAM user within User Group

groupEmptyUsers.^description: {$COUNT} User groups have no users within them. Consider deleting the groups if not being used.

unusedRole.^description: You have {$COUNT} unused roles in your account. Review the necessities of these roles, and delete them if no longer necessary. By removing unused roles, you can simplify monitoring and improve your security posture.

roleLongSession.^description: {$COUNT} role session duration is longer than the default duration of 60 minutes. Unless your applications and/or federated users need to complete longer running workloads in a single session, it is recommended to stick with the default session duration.

hasAlternateContact.^description: Alternate account contacts help AWS get in contact with the appropriate personnel if needed. Configure the account’s alternate contacts to point to a group rather than an individual. For example, create separate email distribution lists for billing, operations, and security and configure these as Billing, Security, and Operations contacts in each active AWS account. This ensures that multiple people will receive AWS notifications and be able to respond, even if someone is on vacation, changes roles, or leaves the company.

noUsersFound.^description: Create individual entities and give unique security credentials and permissions to each user accessing your account. With individual entities and no shared credentials, you can audit the activity of each user.

rootHasAccessKey.^description: The root user is the most privileged user in an AWS account, with full administrative access to all resources within the account, and in some cases cannot be constrained by security policies. Disabling programmatic access to the root user, establishing appropriate controls for the root user, and avoiding routine use of the root user helps reduce the risk of inadvertent exposure of the root credentials and subsequent compromise of the cloud environment. Programmatic access to AWS APIs should never use the root user. It is best not to generate static an access key for the root user. If one already exists, you should transition any processes using that key to use temporary access keys from an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, or, if necessary, static access keys from an IAM user.
rootHasAccessKey.shortDesc: Remove access keys for the root user

supportPlanLowTier.^description: It is recommended that you subscribe to the AWS Business Support tier or higher for all of your AWS production accounts. For more information, refer to Compare AWS Support Plans. If you don't have premium support, you must have an action plan to handle issues which require help from AWS Support. AWS Support provides a mix of tools and technology, people, and programs designed to proactively help you optimize performance, lower costs, and innovate faster. AWS Business Support provides additional benefits including access to AWS Trusted Advisor and AWS Personal Health Dashboard and faster response times.
supportPlanLowTier.shortDesc: Subscribe to the AWS Business Support tier (or higher)

hasAccessKeyNoRotate30days.^description: {$COUNT} user(s) impacted. When you cannot rely on temporary credentials and require long term credentials, rotate the IAM access keys regularly(maximum every 90 days). If an access key is compromised without your knowledge, you limit how long the credentials can be used to access your resources

hasAccessKeyNoRotate90days.^description: {$COUNT} user(s) impacted. When you cannot rely on temporary credentials and require long term credentials, rotate the IAM access keys regularly(maximum every 90 days). If an access key is compromised without your knowledge, you limit how long the credentials can be used to access your resources

enableCostBudget.^description: AWS Budgets enable monitoring of monthly costs and usage with notifications when costs are forecasted to exceed target thresholds. Forecasted cost notifications can provide an indication of unexpected activity, providing extra defense in addition to other monitoring systems, such as AWS Trusted Advisor and Amazon GuardDuty. Monitoring and understanding your AWS costs is also part of good operational hygiene.

enableGuardDuty.^description: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat-detection service that continuously monitors for malicious or unauthorized behavior to help protect your AWS accounts, workloads, and data. When it detects unexpected and potentially malicious activity, GuardDuty delivers detailed security findings for visibility and remediation. GuardDuty can detect threats such as cryptocurrency mining activity, access from Tor clients and relays, unexpected behavior, and compromised IAM credentials. Enable GuardDuty and respond to findings to stop potentially malicious or unauthorized behavior in your AWS environment.

hasExternalIdentityProvider.^description: This enables your users to sign in to the AWS access portal with their corporate credentials. They can then navigate to their assigned accounts, roles, and applications hosted in external IdPs. For example, you can connect an external IdP such as Okta or Azure Active Directory (AD), to IAM Identity Center. Your users can then sign in to the AWS access portal with their existing Okta or Azure credentials. In addition, you can assign access permissions centrally for your users across all the accounts and applications in your AWS organization. In addition, developers can simply sign in to the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) using their existing credentials, and benefit from automatic short-term credential generation and rotation.

hasSSORoles.^description: With AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS Single Sign-On), you can manage sign-in security for your workforce identities, also known as workforce users. IAM Identity Center provides one place where you can create or connect workforce users and centrally manage their access across all their AWS accounts and applications. You can use multi-account permissions to assign your workforce users access to AWS accounts. You can use application assignments to assign your users access to IAM Identity Center enabled applications, cloud applications, and customer Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML 2.0) applications.

rootConsoleLogin30days.^description:
It is critical to prevent root user access from getting into the wrong hands and to be aware whenever root user activity occurs in your AWS account. We recommend that you configure an administrative user in AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS Single Sign-On) to perform daily tasks and access AWS resources. However, you can perform the tasks listed below only when you sign in as the root user of an account.
[1] Change your account settings, [2] Restore IAM user permissions, [3] Activate IAM access to the Billing and Cost Management console, [4] View certain tax invocies, [5] Close your account and etc. Refers to the link
rootConsoleLogin30days.shortDesc: Review activity carry out by root

rootConsoleLoginFail3x.^description:
We detected at least 3 attempts of root id login failure in the past 30 days. Please review CloudTrail in us-east-1 region with the EventName=ConsoleLogin, dive deep into the activity information such as eventTime, sourceIPAddress and userAgent.
Recommend to turn on Amazon GuardDuty to proactively perform such Threat Detection

hasOrganization.^description: This AWS account is not belong to any AWS organization. Recommend to separate workloads using accounts. Establish common guardrails and isolation between environments (such as production, development, and test) and workloads through a multi-account strategy. Account-level separation is strongly recommended, as it provides a strong isolation boundary for security, billing, and access. We need to have an account structure that isolates cloud operations, unrelated workloads, and environments into separate accounts, increasing security across the cloud infrastructure.

userNoActivity90days.^description: {$COUNT} of user(s) does not has active activity in the past 90 days (neither console or api). Please review and disable.

enableCURReport.^description: Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) has not been setup in this accounts. Setup CUR for better cost analysis.

EnableConfigService.^description: AWS Config is not enabled. The AWS Config service performs configuration management of supported AWS resources in your account and delivers log files to you. The recorded information includes the configuration item (AWS resource), relationships between configuration items, and any configuration changes between resources.

PartialEnableConfigService.^description: Not all regions has Config enabled. The AWS Config service performs configuration management of supported AWS resources in your account and delivers log files to you. The recorded information includes the configuration item (AWS resource), relationships between configuration items, and any configuration changes between resources.

SCPEnabled.^description: No service control policy (SCP) other than the default FullAWSAccess is attached anywhere in your AWS Organization (root, organizational units or accounts), or the SCP policy type is not enabled on the root. FullAWSAccess allows everything, so without at least one customer SCP there are no organization-wide guardrails on the maximum permissions of IAM users and roles in member accounts. SCPs are available only when the organization uses All Features. This check reads the organization from the management account or a delegated administrator; from a member account it is reported as not evaluable.

hasAWSBackupPlans.^description: AWS Backup plans are not configured. AWS Backup provides centralized backup management across AWS services including RDS, DynamoDB, EBS, EFS, and more. Configure AWS Backup plans to ensure regular backups are taken automatically based on a periodic schedule. This ensures you have the ability to recover from administrative, logical, or physical error scenarios. AWS Backup simplifies backup management and provides a single place to configure and audit the backup-related activity of your AWS resources.

unusedCustomerManagedPolicy.^description: You have {$COUNT} customer managed policies that are not attached to any IAM users, groups, or roles. These unused policies represent operational clutter and potential security risks if accidentally attached. Review these policies and delete them if they are no longer needed. Regularly removing unused policies helps maintain a clean IAM environment and reduces the attack surface.

iamUsersWithFederationAvailable.^description: {$COUNT} IAM users have long-term credentials (passwords or access keys) while federation (SAML or OIDC) is configured in your account. When federation is available, human users should use federated access with temporary credentials instead of IAM users with long-term credentials. This reduces the risk of credential exposure and aligns with AWS security best practices. Consider migrating these users to federated access through AWS IAM Identity Center or your configured identity provider.
iamUsersWithFederationAvailable.shortDesc: Use federation instead of IAM users

wildcardActionsDetection.^description: {$COUNT} policies contain wildcard actions (e.g., s3:*, ec2:*) beyond full administrator access. While full admin access is sometimes necessary, service-level wildcards grant excessive permissions that violate the principle of least privilege. Review these policies and replace wildcard actions with specific permissions that match the actual requirements. This reduces the risk of unintended access and improves your security posture.
wildcardActionsDetection.shortDesc: Replace wildcard actions with specific permissions

unnecessaryCustomPolicies.^description: {$COUNT} customer managed policies may duplicate functionality available in AWS managed policies. AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS and automatically updated when new services or features are released. Review these custom policies and consider replacing them with AWS managed policies where appropriate. This reduces maintenance burden and ensures your policies stay current with AWS best practices.

missingPolicyConditions.^description: {$COUNT} customer managed policies contain sensitive operations without appropriate security conditions. Sensitive operations such as IAM modifications, security configuration changes, and privilege escalation actions should be protected with conditions like MFA enforcement (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent), IP restrictions (aws:SourceIp), or secure transport requirements (aws:SecureTransport). Adding these conditions provides defense-in-depth by ensuring that even if credentials are compromised, additional security controls must be satisfied before sensitive actions can be performed. Review the identified policies and add appropriate condition blocks to restrict when and how sensitive operations can be executed.
missingPolicyConditions.shortDesc: Add security conditions to policies with sensitive operations

missingPermissionsBoundaries.^description: {$COUNT} IAM users or roles with delegated administration capabilities are missing permissions boundaries. Permissions boundaries are an advanced IAM feature that sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant to an IAM entity. When you delegate administrative permissions to users or roles (such as the ability to create or manage other IAM entities), permissions boundaries provide an additional layer of control by defining the maximum permissions these delegated administrators can have, even if their identity-based policies grant broader access. This helps prevent privilege escalation and ensures that delegated administrators cannot grant themselves or others more permissions than intended. Review the identified entities and apply appropriate permissions boundaries to limit their maximum permissions scope.
missingPermissionsBoundaries.shortDesc: Apply permissions boundaries to delegated administrators

scpBestPractices.^description: One or more organizational units or member accounts in your AWS Organization are missing recommended guardrails in their EFFECTIVE set of service control policies (SCPs attached directly plus those inherited from every parent OU and the root). Best-practice SCP guardrails are: (1) denying root user actions in member accounts, (2) restricting access to approved AWS Regions (aws:RequestedRegion), and (3) preventing privilege escalation by denying sensitive IAM actions such as iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion or iam:PassRole. A guardrail provided by any SCP in the inheritance path counts, so splitting guardrails across several SCPs is fine. The management account is not evaluated because SCPs never apply to it. Review the listed OUs/accounts and attach SCPs with the missing Deny statements at the root or a parent OU.

bedrockLongTermApiKey.^description: You have {$COUNT} IAM users holding active long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys (service-specific credentials for bedrock.amazonaws.com, usually on IAM users named BedrockAPIKey-*). Long-term Bedrock API keys are bearer tokens that grant model invocation without SigV4 signing. If leaked, attackers can use them to run LLM inference on your bill (LLMjacking). Use short-term API keys or IAM role credentials for applications, and delete ALL unused keys and their IAM users. Deleting a key does not delete its IAM user, so when the Bedrock console asks whether to delete the IAM user as well, choose yes.
bedrockLongTermApiKey.shortDesc: Replace long-term Bedrock API keys with short-term credentials

bedrockApiKeyNoExpiry.^description: You have {$COUNT} IAM users with active long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys that never expire. A non-expiring key stays usable until someone deletes it, so a leaked key can be abused indefinitely. Set an expiration when generating keys, and rotate or delete existing keys that never expire.
bedrockApiKeyNoExpiry.shortDesc: Set an expiration on long-term Bedrock API keys

bedrockApiKeyUnusedUser.^description: You have {$COUNT} IAM users left over from long-term Amazon Bedrock API keys. They have no active key (all keys are expired, inactive, or deleted), but deleting a key does not delete its IAM user or the attached Bedrock permissions such as AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess. Anyone with IAM permissions can generate a new key on the user. This happens when a key is only deactivated, expires, or is deleted without also deleting the IAM user (the Bedrock console prompts for this when you delete a key). Confirm the user has no other credentials in use, then delete ALL unused keys and their IAM users.
bedrockApiKeyUnusedUser.shortDesc: Delete IAM users left over from unused Bedrock API keys
ref: [Remove unused users, roles, permissions, policies, and credentials]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#remove-credentials>

orgMgmtAccountHostsWorkloads.^description: The AWS Organizations management account hosts workload resources (EC2 instances, Lambda functions, RDS DB instances or EKS clusters) in the scanned Regions. The management account cannot be restricted by service control policies and holds organization-wide privileges, so workloads running there are outside your guardrails and widen the blast radius of a compromise. Use the management account only for organization, billing and identity administration and move workloads into member accounts. Functions deployed by AWS Control Tower, Landing Zone Accelerator and Quick Setup are excluded.
orgMgmtAccountHostsWorkloads.shortDesc: Move workloads out of the management account

orgNotAllFeatures.^description: Your AWS Organization uses only the consolidated billing feature set. Without All Features you cannot use service control policies, resource control policies, tag, backup or declarative policies, or centralized root access, so no organization-wide guardrails can be enforced. Enable all features in AWS Organizations (every member account must approve, or accounts created by the organization are switched automatically).
orgNotAllFeatures.shortDesc: Enable all features in AWS Organizations

orgMemberAlternateContactsMissing.^description: One or more member accounts in your AWS Organization are missing SECURITY, BILLING or OPERATIONS alternate contacts. AWS sends security notifications, abuse reports and billing or operational notices to these contacts; when they are missing, only the root user email of each account is notified. Set alternate contacts (ideally distribution lists) for every member account centrally from the management account or the AWS Account Management delegated administrator. Requires trusted access for AWS Account Management; from a member account this check is not evaluable.
orgMemberAlternateContactsMissing.shortDesc: Set alternate contacts for all member accounts
ref: [Update alternate contacts for any account in your organization]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/accounts/latest/reference/manage-acct-update-contact-alternate.html>

orgNoResourceControlPolicies.^description: No resource control policy (RCP) enforces an organization data perimeter. Either the RCP policy type is not enabled on the organization root, only the default RCPFullAWSAccess is attached, or no attached RCP has a Deny statement conditioned on aws:PrincipalOrgID / aws:ResourceOrgID / aws:SourceOrgID (or the OrgPaths variants). RCPs centrally restrict which principals can access resources such as S3 buckets, KMS keys, SQS queues and Secrets Manager secrets in member accounts, preventing access from identities outside your organization even when a resource policy is misconfigured.
orgNoResourceControlPolicies.shortDesc: Enforce a data perimeter with RCPs

orgNoTagPolicy.^description: No AWS Organizations tag policy is attached to the root, an OU or an account (or the tag policy type is not enabled). Tag policies standardize tag keys and values, such as a data-classification key, across accounts so resources can be identified, governed and protected according to their sensitivity. The detail shows whether any attached tag policy defines a classification-like tag key (name-based, informational only).
orgNoTagPolicy.shortDesc: Attach a tag policy (e.g. data classification)

orgOuStructureFlat.^description: Your AWS Organization has no organizational units, or member accounts are attached directly to the organization root. Without an OU structure (for example Security, Infrastructure, Workloads, Sandbox) you cannot apply different guardrails to different environments, and every policy must be attached at the root or per account. Group accounts into OUs by function and compliance requirements rather than by reporting structure.

rootCentralizedAccessNotEnabled.^description: Centralized root access for member accounts is not enabled (IAM ListOrganizationsFeatures does not report RootCredentialsManagement and RootSessions). With centralized root access you can remove root user credentials from member accounts, prevent their recovery, and perform the few root-only tasks through short-lived privileged sessions from the management account or a delegated administrator. Enable trusted access for IAM and both features in the IAM console.

scpNoBackupTamperProtection.^description: No attached service control policy denies the AWS Backup actions used to tamper with backups (backup:DeleteBackupVault, DeleteBackupVaultAccessPolicy, DeleteBackupVaultLockConfiguration, DeleteRecoveryPoint, PutBackupVaultAccessPolicy, UpdateRecoveryPointLifecycle). Ransomware actors with administrator access in a member account commonly delete recovery points or shorten retention before encrypting data. Attach an SCP that denies these actions except for a designated backup administration role, and consider AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode for immutable backups.
scpNoBackupTamperProtection.shortDesc: Protect backups from tampering with an SCP

scpNoDataProtectionGuardrail.^description: No attached service control policy (SCP) denies the actions that weaken account-wide data-protection settings: changing S3 Block Public Access (s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock / s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock), disabling EBS encryption by default (ec2:DisableEbsEncryptionByDefault) and scheduling KMS key deletion (kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion). Without these preventive guardrails any administrator in a member account can expose data publicly, create unencrypted volumes or destroy keys protecting encrypted data. Attach an SCP that denies these actions (with an exception for a designated platform role if needed). A Deny that only applies to the root user or outside approved Regions does not count. Region restriction is reported by scpBestPractices.
scpNoDataProtectionGuardrail.shortDesc: Protect data-protection settings with an SCP

scpNoIamUserCreationDeny.^description: No attached service control policy (SCP) denies iam:CreateUser or iam:CreateAccessKey. IAM users with long-term access keys are a common source of credential leaks; organizations that federate human access through IAM Identity Center should prevent new IAM users and access keys in workload accounts with an SCP (optionally with an exception for an approved automation role or only on selected OUs).
scpNoIamUserCreationDeny.shortDesc: Restrict IAM user and access key creation with an SCP

scpNoSecurityServiceProtection.^description: No attached service control policy (SCP) fully prevents security services from being disabled. The detail lists which of these are not denied: CloudTrail (cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail), GuardDuty (guardduty:DeleteDetector, guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount / DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount), AWS Config (config:StopConfigurationRecorder, config:DeleteConfigurationRecorder) and leaving the organization (organizations:LeaveOrganization). An attacker or careless administrator in a member account can otherwise switch off logging and detection. A Deny that only applies to the root user or outside approved Regions does not count.
scpNoSecurityServiceProtection.shortDesc: Prevent disabling security services with an SCP

securityServicesNoDelegatedAdmin.^description: Security services are administered from the organization management account: either no delegated administrator is registered for any of GuardDuty, Security Hub, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer or AWS Config, or a service has organization trusted access enabled but no delegated administrator. Delegate security services to a dedicated security tooling account so the management account is used as little as possible.
securityServicesNoDelegatedAdmin.shortDesc: Delegate security services to a security tooling account
ref: [AWS services that you can use with AWS Organizations]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_integrate_services_list.html>

ssoAssignmentsToIndividualUsers.^description: IAM Identity Center permission sets are assigned to individual users instead of groups. Direct user assignments are hard to review and are often left behind when people change roles. Assign permission sets to groups (ideally synchronized from your identity provider) and keep individual assignments only for documented break-glass access.
ssoAssignmentsToIndividualUsers.shortDesc: Assign Identity Center permission sets to groups
ref: [Assign user or group access to AWS accounts]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/assignusers.html>

ssoPermissionSetOverprivileged.^description: IAM Identity Center permission sets allow sessions longer than 8 hours. Long sessions keep credentials valid long after work is done and increase the impact of a stolen session. The detail also lists admin-level permission sets (AdministratorAccess or an inline Allow *:*) so their audience can be reviewed.

thirdPartyRoleNoExternalId.^description: {$COUNT} IAM roles trust an AWS account outside your organization without requiring a strong sts:ExternalId (missing, IfExists, wildcard, shorter than 8 characters, numeric-only or equal to an account ID) or an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition. Third parties that assume roles in many customer accounts must be given a unique external ID to prevent the confused deputy problem.
thirdPartyRoleNoExternalId.shortDesc: Require a unique sts:ExternalId for third-party roles
ref: [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html>

thirdPartyRoleOverprivileged.^description: {$COUNT} IAM roles trusted by an AWS account outside your organization have admin-level permissions (AdministratorAccess, IAMFullAccess, or a policy allowing *, *:* or iam:* on all resources). A compromise at the third party then becomes full control of your account. Grant third-party roles only the permissions the vendor documents as required.
ref: [Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties]<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html>
